vignette:
He is 21, European, single, and works now as a bus driver, though he speaks about the work almost as if it is something he stumbled into after another life ended too early. When he tells the story of his trauma, he begins in the military, where he is still very young and trying to prove he can keep up. He remembers the early months as harsh but manageable: long hours, cold mornings, the constant pressure to stay alert, to not be the one who flinches. He learns quickly how to sleep lightly, how to scan a room before sitting down, how to keep his face neutral even when his body is tense.

The event that stays with him happens during deployment, in a stretch of time he describes as “all noise and waiting.” He is on patrol when an explosion tears through the routine of the day. He remembers the sharp, white instant of fear before sound returns, then the confusion of dust, shouting, and the impossible task of understanding who is hurt and where. One of the men near him is killed. Another is badly injured. He says that in the moments after, everything feels slowed and unreal, as if he is watching the scene from a little way outside his own body. He moves because others move, because training demands it, but later he cannot remember the exact sequence of what he did. What remains vivid are fragments: the smell of burned metal, the ringing in his ears, the look on a fellow soldier’s face when he realizes someone is not getting up.

Afterward, he is not the same in a way that is hard for him to explain to people who were never there. At first he thinks he just needs time. He tells himself the shaking in his hands, the tightness in his chest, the jumpiness when doors slam are temporary. But the memories do not stay in the past. They arrive uninvited, often when he is trying to fall asleep or when something ordinary catches him off guard. A loud bang outside his flat can send him right back to the patrol route, his body already braced before his mind catches up. He wakes at night drenched in sweat, heart pounding, not always from a clear nightmare, but from a feeling that danger is close. Sometimes the dreams are specific: the blast, the dust, the wounded man calling out. Sometimes they are less clear and more terrible because of it, leaving him with dread he cannot place.

He starts avoiding things without fully admitting that he is avoiding them. He does not want to talk much about the deployment, especially not with friends who ask casual questions and expect a simple answer. He stops watching war films and clicks away from news stories about conflict. He notices that he chooses his seat carefully in cafes, always facing the door. He dislikes crowds, especially in narrow places where he cannot see who is behind him. He used to enjoy the noise of being around other young men, the banter and rough joking, but now he finds himself withdrawing, saying less, leaving early, pretending to be tired. He feels detached from people his own age, as if they are living in a different tempo from his own.

Working as a bus driver gives him structure, but it also keeps him on edge. He is good at the job because it requires vigilance, routes, schedules, and the ability to stay composed, yet it also means he spends long hours listening for trouble and watching mirrors and traffic with a kind of hyperalertness that never fully switches off. A backfiring car or a sudden shout at a stop makes his whole body tense. He grips the wheel harder than he wants to, jaw clenched, scanning for danger before he can tell himself he is safe. On difficult days he feels irritated with passengers for the smallest things, and afterward he is ashamed of how quickly his temper rises. He also notices how tired he is, not just physically but in a deeper sense, as though he is carrying an invisible weight that started overseas and has followed him home.

He has not found an easy way to put the experience into words. He can describe the explosion in detail, but not the way it changed the shape of his life. He says he feels “stuck” in that period, not all the time, but often enough that it affects how he moves through his days. Even now, months later, he is still measuring every sound, every shadow, every sudden movement against that one moment when everything split open.
